title: File I/O Details - Title Slide
summary: Title slide introducing Unit 5h on File I/O Details, taught by Mark Redekopp as part of CS103.
main_text: This unit covers File I/O Details in C++. The lecture is part of CS103 and is presented by Mark Redekopp. Topics include file streams review, computer organization, binary vs text files, file pointer manipulation, I/O redirection, and C-style file I/O.
notes_text: This unit builds on the stream concepts from Unit 5g and dives deeper into the mechanics of file I/O, including low-level details about how files are stored and accessed, and alternative approaches like I/O redirection.

title: Review: File I/O Using C++ Streams - Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing a review of how programs directly access data in files using C++ streams.
main_text: This section reviews how your program can directly access data in files using C++ streams, covering ifstream and ofstream objects, the fstream library, and basic file reading and writing operations.
notes_text: This review section sets the foundation for the more advanced file I/O topics covered later in the unit, including binary file I/O, file pointer manipulation, and I/O redirection.

title: File Streams Review
summary: C++ uses ifstream (counterpart to cin) and ofstream (counterpart to cout) from the fstream library to read from and write to files.
main_text: C++ leverages the SAME interface that cin and cout provide to: Read data IN from a file (like cin, but data comes from a file not the keyboard) and Write data OUT to a file (like cout, but data goes to a file not the terminal). The counterpart to cin is an ifstream object. The counterpart to cout is an ofstream object. To read: #include <iostream>, #include <fstream>, Using namespace std; ifstream ifile("dat1.txt"); ifile >> x; ifile.close();. To write: ofstream ofile("dat2.txt"); ofile << "Hi there" << std::endl; ofile.close();. The ifstream reads from the file through the OS into input stream memory, while ofstream writes from output stream memory through the OS to the file.
notes_text: This is a review from Unit 5g. The key point is that file streams use the exact same operators and interface as cin/cout, thanks to inheritance in the C++ stream class hierarchy. Always include both <iostream> and <fstream>.

images.description: Diagram showing ifstream reading from dat1.txt through OS into input stream memory, and ofstream writing from output stream memory through OS to dat2.txt, with code examples for each.

title: Recall: Getting Data from Files
summary: To process file data in a program, you must first read it into a C/C++ variable. Everything that follows is about getting data into variables.
main_text: IF you want your program to operate on data from a file, THEN you MUST read it into a C/C++ variable before processing it. Everything we will see subsequently is simply how to get data into a variable. After that we can just process it normally. This fundamental principle applies to all file I/O: the program cannot operate directly on file data; it must first be loaded into memory (RAM) through variables.
notes_text: This slide emphasizes a key concept that students sometimes overlook: files live on disk, but programs operate on data in RAM. The various I/O techniques covered in this unit are all just different ways to transfer data from disk to RAM variables.

title: Computer Organization
summary: The processor can only talk directly to RAM, not to disk. The C++ library and OS provide routines to translate between RAM and file data on disk.
main_text: Why can't we just process data in a file directly? Because the processor can only talk directly to RAM / memory. It needs "translation" to access data on the hard drive or other disk. All code and data resides in RAM. RAM stores all variables / data that your program accesses. How do we access files? The C++ library and the OS provide routines to perform the translation to read/write data from RAM to a file. Memory is organized with Code at the top, then Globals, Heap in the middle, and Stack at the bottom. The processor works with ints, strings, etc. in RAM. ifstream and ofstream objects facilitate the transfer between RAM and Disk, where data files (.ppt, .txt, .docx) are stored as binary (110010101001...).
notes_text: This slide provides important context about computer architecture. Students need to understand that the CPU cannot directly access disk storage - all data must pass through RAM. This is why we need file I/O operations to bridge the gap between persistent storage (disk) and working memory (RAM).

images.description: Diagram showing computer organization: processor (Apple M4) at top connecting to RAM (memory layout with Code, Globals, Heap, Stack sections). RAM connects bidirectionally to Disk storage. Data files (.ppt, .txt, .docx) are shown on disk as binary. ifstream/ofstream facilitate RAM-to-Disk transfer.

title: Starting File I/O
summary: File I/O has two operations: reading (Open command using ifstream) and writing (Save As command using ofstream), both requiring close() when done.
main_text: Just like a document or image editor allows two operations on files: Read info from the file (like 'Open' command): Use an 'ifstream' object to open the file, Read data from the file, Close it when you're done. Write info to the file (like 'Save As' command): Use an 'ofstream' object, Write the data to a file, Close it when you're done. This maps directly to the everyday experience of opening files in applications and saving them.
notes_text: The analogy to Open and Save As commands makes file I/O intuitive. The three-step pattern (open, read/write, close) should become second nature. Forgetting to close files can lead to data loss for output files because buffered data may not be flushed to disk.

title: Two Kinds of Files: Binary and Text
summary: Files are either text (ASCII character sequences) or binary (raw bit patterns). Text stores 172 as three ASCII chars; binary stores it as 4 bytes directly.
main_text: We conceive of files as "streams" (1D arrays) of data. Files are broken into two types based on how they represent the given information. Text files: File is just a large sequence of ASCII characters (every piece of data is just a byte). Binary files: Data in the file is just bits that can be retrieved in different size chunks (4-byte int, 8-byte double, etc.). Example: Store the number 172 in a file. Text: Would store 3 ASCII chars '1','7','2' (ASCII 49, 55, 50) requiring 3 bytes (but the key is each digit or character is stored separately in ASCII). Binary: If 172 was in an 'int' variable we could store it as 4-bytes in binary rather than separate ASCII characters. In this unit, we will only focus on text file I/O.
notes_text: Understanding the difference between text and binary files is fundamental. Text files are human-readable and portable but less efficient for numeric data. Binary files are compact and fast but not human-readable and can have portability issues (endianness, struct padding).

title: Text File I/O - ifstream / ofstream
summary: Complete example showing ifstream reading from input.txt and ofstream writing to output.txt, with error checking using fail() after open and after read.
main_text: Must include <fstream>. Use ofstream object/variable for writing to a file - can do anything 'cout' can do. Use '>>' operator, I/O manipulators, etc. on the stream but realize operations are happening on data from the file. Close all filestreams using the .close() member function. Complete example: #include <iostream> #include <fstream> using namespace std; int main() { int x; double y; ifstream ifile("input.txt"); if(ifile.fail()){ // able to open file? cout << "Couldn't open file" << endl; return 1; } ifile >> x >> y; if(ifile.fail()){ cout << "Unable to read int & double." << endl; return 1; } ofstream ofile("output.txt"); ofile << "Int from file is " << x << endl; ofile << "Double from file is " << y << endl; ifile.close(); ofile.close(); return 0; }. With input.txt containing '5 -3.5', output.txt gets 'Int from file is 5' and 'Double from file is -3.5'.
notes_text: This example demonstrates best practices: check fail() after opening the file AND after reading data. The two-stage error checking catches both file-not-found errors and data format errors. Always close both input and output file streams.

title: File Location/Pointers and Input Operators - Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing topics about file pointer positioning and input operator behavior differences.
main_text: This section covers file location tracking with file pointers, the differences between operator>>, get(), and peek() for reading from streams, and how to manipulate the file pointer position using seekg() and tellg().
notes_text: Understanding file pointer manipulation is essential for non-sequential file access. This section also clarifies the subtle but important differences between >>, get(), and peek() in terms of whitespace handling and pointer advancement.

title: Error Recovery: Clear() and Ignore()
summary: Use cin.clear() to reset the fail bit after an error, and cin.ignore() to discard bad input from the stream, enabling retry loops for input validation.
main_text:
We use the fail() member function of input streams to DETECT ERRORS. When an operation fails, the input stream sets an internal flag bit (FAIL bit). But this bit STAYS ON even if subsequent operations succeed! We must CLEAR that fail bit using cin.clear(). However, the data in the input stream stays there and will continue to cause us to fail if we don't throw it away using the cin.ignore() function. cin.ignore() takes a maximum number of characters to throw away or a delimiter to stop on ('
'). E.g. cin.ignore(256, '
'). Example: int x; cout << "Enter an int: " << endl; cin >> x; // User enters "ab", cin has 'a','b','
', fail=1. while(cin.fail()) { cin.clear(); // turn off fail flag cin.ignore(256, '
'); // clear inputs cout << "I said enter an int: "; cin >> x; } // After user enters "8", cin has '
', fail=0. cout << "Nice! X = " << x << endl;
notes_text: This is a crucial pattern for robust input validation. The three-step recovery is: 1) clear() to reset status bits, 2) ignore() to discard bad data, 3) re-prompt and re-read. Without ignore(), the bad data stays in the buffer and causes an infinite loop of failures.

images.description: Two cin state diagrams showing status bits. First state: cin contains 'a','b','\n' with fail=1, eof=0, bad=0. After clear and ignore, then user enters '8': cin contains '\n' with fail=0, eof=0, bad=0.

metadata.topic: Error Recovery with Clear and Ignore

title: File Streams and EOF
summary: The ifstream uses a file pointer (fp/getp) to track position. EOF and fail bits are set when reading past the end of file, and fail() is the simplest check.
main_text: Your ifstream object implicitly keeps track of where you are in the file using a file pointer (fp) or get pointer (getp). EOF (end-of-file) or other error means no more data can be read. Use the fail() function to ensure the file is okay for reading/writing. Input streams also allow you to check if you've read the EOF character by calling an eof() function, but fail will be set when eof is and so it's easier to just use fail(). Example trace with file '...The End!EOF': Initially fp at start, fail=0, eof=0, bad=0. After char c; ifile >> c; reads characters successfully, fail=0, eof=0, bad=0. After reading past '!' to hit EOF: fail=1, eof=1, bad=0.
notes_text: The relationship between eof() and fail() is important: when eof is set, fail is also set. So checking fail() alone is sufficient for most use cases. This simplifies code since you only need one check instead of two.

images.description: Three-stage diagram of disk contents '...The End!EOF' with file pointer position and status bits at each stage. Stage 1: fp before content, bits all 0. Stage 2: fp at '!', bits all 0. Stage 3: fp past EOF, fail=1, eof=1, bad=0.

title: operator>> vs. get()
summary: operator>> skips leading whitespace and stops at trailing whitespace. The get() function reads raw characters including whitespace without skipping.
main_text: operator>> skips leading whitespace and stops at trailing whitespace. In the example with file text 'I t   6 7 8 ...': string s; ifile >> s; returns "It" and stops at the space. The spaces will NOT be read in - they will be skipped by operator>>. Then char x; ifile >> x; skips the space and gives x='6'. To get raw data from the file (including whitespaces) use the get() function. get() reads the very next character regardless of whether it is whitespace, giving you full control over what is read from the stream.
notes_text: This distinction is critical when processing files where whitespace is meaningful (like counting characters, preserving formatting, or reading binary-like data in text mode). Use >> when you want tokens, use get() when you want every character.

images.description: File text diagram showing 'I t   6 7 8 ...' with fp/getp positions. After >> extracts 'It', fp points past 't'. After >> extracts char, it skips space and gets '6'. get() would read the space instead.

title: get vs. peek
summary: get() returns the character at getp and advances the pointer. peek() returns the character at getp but does NOT advance the pointer.
main_text: To get raw data from the file (including whitespaces) use the ifstream::get() function. It returns the character at the getp and moves getp on by one. Example: char c = ifile.get(); returns 'I' and advances getp. c = ifile.get(); returns ' ' (space) and advances getp again. To see what the next character is without moving the "getp" pointer on to the next character, use ifstream::peek() function. It returns the character at the getp but does NOT move getp on. Example with file text 'I   c a n   ...': ifile >> c; returns 'I'. ifile >> c; skips space and returns 'c'. But c = ifile.peek(); returns 'I' and doesn't move to next char - the pointer stays in place. This is useful for lookahead operations.
notes_text: peek() is invaluable when you need to make decisions based on the next character without consuming it. Common use cases include: determining whether to read an int or string, checking for end-of-line, and implementing simple parsers that need lookahead.

images.description: File text diagram showing 'I   c a n   ...' with getp positions after various operations. get() advances the pointer with each call. peek() returns the character without advancing. >> skips whitespace before reading.

title: Changing File Pointer Location (ifstream) - seekg and tellg
summary: seekg() jumps to a specific byte position in a file using offset from beginning, current position, or end. tellg() returns the current byte offset.
main_text: Rather than read sequentially in a file we often need to jump around to particular byte locations. ifstream::seekg(): Go to a particular byte location. Pass an offset relative from current position or absolute byte from start or end of file. To specify what the offset is relative to, use one of ios_base::beg/cur/end. ifstream::tellg(): Return the current location's byte-offset from the beginning of the file. Example with file 'It was the best of...EOF': seekg(9, ios_base::beg) moves getp to byte 9 (the 'b' in 'best'). With getp at byte 9, tellg() returns 9. seekg(-4, ios_base::cur) moves getp back 4 bytes from current position. The 2nd arg to seekg(): ios_base::beg = position from beginning of file. ios_base::cur = position relative to current location. ios_base::end = position relative from end of file (i.e. 0 or negative number).
notes_text: seekg and tellg enable random access to file contents, which is essential for binary file processing, implementing search functionality, or re-reading portions of a file. The byte offset is 0-indexed from the beginning of the file.

images.description: File content diagram showing 'It was the best of...EOF' with byte positions labeled 0,1,2,...9,...3123. Arrows show seekg(9, ios_base::beg) moving to position 9, and seekg(-4, ios_base::cur) moving backward from current position. ios_base::begin and ios_base::end markers are shown at file boundaries.

title: Changing File Pointer Location - Code Example
summary: Complete code example demonstrating seekg and tellg to find file size, read specific bytes, and navigate forward and backward in a file.
main_text: Complete example: int main(int argc, char *argv[]) { int size; char c; ifstream fstr("stuff.txt"); fstr.seekg(0, ios_base::end); // go to end size = fstr.tellg(); // get file size cout << "File size (bytes)=" << size << endl; fstr.seekg(1, ios_base::beg); // go to byte 1 cout << "2nd byte in file is "; fstr >> c; cout << c << endl; fstr.seekg(-2, ios_base::cur); // go back 2 cout << "1st byte in file is "; fstr >> c; cout << c << endl; fstr.close(); return 0; }. The diagram shows: initially getp at position 0 of 'It was the best of...'. seekg(0, ios_base::end) moves to EOF at position 3123. seekg(1, ios_base::beg) moves to position 1, reading 't'. seekg(-2, ios_base::cur) moves back to position 0, reading 'I'.
notes_text: The pattern of seekg(0, ios_base::end) followed by tellg() is the standard way to determine file size in C++. Note that after seekg to the end, you must seek back before reading. The -2 offset from cur accounts for the character just read plus one more position back.

images.description: Three disk diagrams showing file content 'It was the best of...' with getp positions at different stages: initially at 0, after seekg to end at position 3123, after seekg(1, beg) at position 1, and after seekg(-2, cur) back at position 0.

title: Binary File I/O - Section Header
summary: Section divider for Binary File I/O content, marked as material students are not responsible for.
main_text: This section covers Binary File I/O, which deals with reading and writing raw binary data to files rather than text. Students are not responsible for this material on exams, but it provides useful background on how binary files work and when they might be preferred over text files.
notes_text: While marked as not required, binary file I/O is commonly used in professional software for performance-critical applications, database storage, and handling non-text data like images and audio.

title: Binary vs. Text File I/O
summary: Binary files store raw memory bits directly to disk. Text files store the ASCII representation of data as it would be printed.
main_text: Binary file content takes the literal bits from memory/RAM and saves it to a file. Text file content is the ASCII representation of the data (as it would be printed). Example with struct Student { char name[40]; int major; double gpa; }; and s1 with name="Jill", major=5, gpa=3.7. In memory at address 7300: name stores 4a696c6c (hex for 'Jill'), major at 7340 stores 00000005, gpa at 7344 stores c0100000 00000000. Binary File Content: writes the exact bytes from memory: 4a696c6c, 00 ? ? ?, ..., 00000005, c0100000, 00000000. Text File Content: writes ASCII characters: 4A 69 6C 6C 20 35 20 34 2E 30 0A (which reads as 'Jill 5 4.0\n').
notes_text: Binary files are more compact for numeric data (4 bytes for any int vs variable bytes for text) and faster to read/write since no conversion is needed. However, they are not human-readable and may not be portable across different hardware architectures.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison showing a Student struct in memory (with hex addresses and byte values), and how it would be stored as binary file content (raw bytes) vs text file content (ASCII characters 'Jill 5 4.0').

title: Binary File I/O Functions
summary: Binary files use ios::binary mode flag, write() to output raw bytes, and read() to input raw bytes, both requiring char* pointers and byte counts.
main_text: When opening the file, include the "binary" mode flag: open(const char* filename, ios_base::openmode mode). In addition to the filename argument, provide ios::binary. To write data to a binary file use the write() function: ostream& ostream::write(const char* s, streamsize n); where s = pointer to the starting address of the data to write to the file, should be cast to a char*, and n = the number of bytes to be written = number_of_elements * size_of_element. To read data from a binary file use the read() function: istream& istream::read(char* s, streamsize n); where s = a pointer to where you want the data read from the file to be placed in memory (this pointer should be cast to a char*), and n = Number of bytes you want to read.
notes_text: The static_cast<char*> is necessary because write() and read() work with raw bytes, not typed data. The programmer is responsible for calculating the correct byte count, typically using sizeof() and element count. Incorrect byte counts lead to corruption.

title: Copy a File (Binary)
summary: Complete example of copying a file using binary I/O: determine file size with seekg/tellg, allocate buffer, read entire file, write to new file.
main_text: Complete binary file copy example: #include <iostream> #include <fstream> using namespace std; int main() { std::ifstream infile("src.txt", ios::binary); std::ofstream outfile("copy.txt", ios::binary); infile.seekg(0, infile.end); // get size of file long size = infile.tellg(); infile.seekg(0); // allocate memory for file content char* buffer = new char[size]; // read content of infile infile.read(buffer, size); // write to outfile outfile.write(buffer, size); // release dynamically-allocated memory delete[] buffer; outfile.close(); infile.close(); return 0; }. This demonstrates: opening in binary mode, determining file size, dynamic memory allocation for the buffer, reading the entire file at once, and writing it out.
notes_text: This example combines several concepts: binary file mode, seekg/tellg for file size, dynamic memory allocation with new/delete, and read/write for binary I/O. In practice, you would add error checking after open and after read/write operations.

title: Binary File I/O with Structs
summary: write() and read() can save/load arrays of structs to binary files using static_cast<char*> and sizeof() to calculate byte counts.
main_text: write() is a member of ofstream. Pass a pointer to the starting location of the data to write to the file (should be cast to a char*) and the number of bytes to be written = number_of_elements * size_of_element. read() is a member of ifstream. Pass a pointer to where you want the data read from the file to be placed in memory (this pointer should be cast to char*). Pass the number of bytes you want to read. Example with struct Student { char name[40]; int major; double gpa; };: void saveToFile(const char* fname, Student* data) { ofstream ofile(fname, ios::binary); ofile.write(static_cast<char*>(data), 100*sizeof(Student)); ofile.close(); } void readFromFile(const char* fname, Student* data) { ifstream ifile(fname, ios::binary); ifile.read(static_cast<char*>(data), 100*sizeof(Student)); ifile.close(); }. In main: Student stu[100]; saveToFile("class.dat", stu); Student duplicate[100]; readFromFile("class.dat", duplicate);
notes_text: This pattern is very efficient for saving and loading large arrays of structured data. The entire array is written/read in a single operation. However, structs with pointers (like std::string members) cannot be safely written this way because the pointers would be meaningless when read back.

title: I/O Redirection - Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing I/O Redirection, an OS-level mechanism for redirecting program input/output to/from files.
main_text: This section covers I/O Redirection, an operating system mechanism that allows redirecting the standard input (stdin/cin) to read from a file and standard output (stdout/cout) to write to a file, without modifying the program code.
notes_text: I/O redirection is a powerful Unix/Linux concept that enables programs written with cin/cout to work with files without any code changes. This is fundamental to shell scripting and command-line workflows.

title: Overview: File Streams vs I/O Redirection
summary: Two methods for file I/O: file streams (ifstream/ofstream in C++ code) and I/O redirection (OS-level mechanism using cin/cout with file redirect).
main_text: Two methods for file I/O: File streams (ifstream and ofstream) are part of the C++ library and perform file I/O directly through a cin- and cout-like interface (Covered in Unit 3). I/O redirection: The OS reads or writes data to/from a file by controlling cin and cout. The program just performs normal cin and cout commands. Covered in this unit. With file streams, the program explicitly opens a file: ifstream ifile; ifile >> x >> y;. With I/O redirection, the OS feeds file contents to cin: $ ./app1 < data.txt, and the program just uses cin >> x >> y; as if reading from the keyboard. Both approaches result in the program variables getting the same values (x=15, y=21 from data.txt containing '15 21 hello').
notes_text: I/O redirection is transparent to the program - it does not know whether input comes from a keyboard or a file. This makes programs more versatile since the same code works for interactive use and batch processing.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison diagram. Left: file streams approach with ifstream reading directly from data.txt on disk. Right: I/O redirection approach where OS feeds data.txt contents to cin, and the program reads from cin as normal. Both produce x=15, y=21.

title: I/O Redirection Overview
summary: I/O Redirection is an OS mechanism that redirects file contents into stdin (cin) and redirects stdout (cout) output to a file, without changing program code.
main_text: A second method (other than ifstream and ofstream objects) is to use an OS mechanism called I/O Redirection. All general operating systems support this mechanism. The OS can: Redirect the contents of a file into stdin (i.e. cin), so the program reads from the file through cin as if it were keyboard input. Redirect the output sent to stdout (i.e. cout) to a file rather than the terminal, so program output goes to a file instead of the screen. The program code remains unchanged - it still uses cin and cout normally.
notes_text: I/O redirection is handled entirely by the operating system shell (bash, zsh, etc.), not by the C++ program. This means any program that uses cin/cout can benefit from redirection without modification. This is a key design principle of Unix-like systems.

title: Redirection and Pipes
summary: Shell operators: < redirects file to stdin, > redirects stdout to file, | pipes one program's stdout to another's stdin.
main_text: The OS (Linux or Windows or Mac) provides the following abilities at the command line. < redirect contents of a file as input (stdin) to program: ./simulation < input.txt - OS places contents of input.txt into 'stdin' input stream which the program can access via 'cin'. > redirect program output to a file: ./simulation < input.txt > results.txt - OS takes output from 'stdout' produced by cout and writes them into a new output file on the hard drive: results.txt. | pipe output of first program to second: stdout of first program is then used as stdin of next program. This allows chaining programs together where one program's output feeds directly into another's input.
notes_text: These three operators (<, >, |) are fundamental shell concepts. The pipe operator is especially powerful - it enables the Unix philosophy of composing small, focused programs into complex workflows. Each program does one thing well and pipes connect them.

title: Redirection and Pipe Examples (Input)
summary: Practical examples: ./shapes < input.txt redirects input, with a Codio demo for Exercise 6 - I/O Redirection using randgen and average programs.
main_text: $ ./shapes < input.txt - Redirects contents of input.txt to stdin (i.e. cin) in HW2 shapes program. input.txt contains: 0 10 10 100 50 / 0 200 220 20 30 / 1 80 180 25 25 / 1 180 50 30 60 / 2. Codio Demo: Go to Codio and find the Exercise 6 - I/O Redirection. From the terminal, compile the programs: $ make randgen and $ make average. Run them without using redirection and pipes: $ ./randgen 20 10 - Notice 20 values between 1-10 are output on stdout/cout. $ ./average - Now type in a list of numbers followed by typing Ctrl-D.
notes_text: This hands-on exercise demonstrates the practical value of I/O redirection. The shapes program reads geometric shape parameters from stdin, and by redirecting input.txt, you can automate the input process instead of typing interactively.

title: Redirection and Pipe Examples (Output and Pipes)
summary: Output redirection (>) saves stdout to a file. Input redirection (<) feeds a file to stdin. Pipes (|) connect one program's output to another's input.
main_text: Output Redirection (>): $ ./randgen 20 10 > out.txt - Now inspect out.txt contents. What would have displayed on the screen is now in out.txt. Input redirection (<): $ ./average < out.txt - The output captured from randgen is now used as input to average. Pipes (|): $ ./randgen 20 10 | ./average - The output of randgen is fed as input to average. This eliminates the intermediate file - randgen's stdout goes directly to average's stdin through the pipe. The pipe is the most elegant solution when you want to chain two programs together.
notes_text: The progression from output redirection to input redirection to pipes shows increasingly elegant solutions to the same problem. Pipes are preferred when you do not need to inspect the intermediate data, as they avoid creating temporary files.

title: Background on C File I/O - Section Header (Not Covered)
summary: Section divider for background material on C-style file I/O, marked as not covered in the course.
main_text: This section provides background on C-style file I/O using FILE pointers and functions like fopen, fclose, fgetc, fgets, fprintf, fscanf. This material is not covered on exams but provides useful context for understanding legacy C code and the foundations of C++ stream I/O.
notes_text: C-style file I/O is still widely used in systems programming and legacy codebases. Understanding it helps when reading older code or working with C libraries from C++ programs.

title: C Style I/O - Section Header
summary: Section divider for C Style I/O, marked as material students are not responsible for.
main_text: This section covers C-style I/O functions as supplementary material. Students are not responsible for this material. It covers the C standard library approach to file I/O using FILE pointers, fopen/fclose, and related functions.
notes_text: While not required for the course, C-style I/O is important for understanding how file operations work at a lower level than C++ streams, and for working with C libraries.

title: FILE* Variables
summary: C uses FILE* pointers with fopen() to open files and fclose() to close them. fopen takes a filename and mode string (r/w/a/rb/wb).
main_text: To access files, C (with the help of the OS) has a data type called 'FILE' which tracks all information and is used to access a single file from your program. You declare a pointer to this FILE type (FILE *). You "open" a file for access using fopen(). Pass it a filename string (char *) and a string indicating read vs. write, text vs. binary. Returns an initialized file pointer or NULL if there was an error opening file. You "close" a file when finished with fclose(). Pass the file pointer. Both of these functions are defined in stdio.h. Example: FILE *fp; fp = fopen("stuff.txt","r"); if(fp == NULL){ printf("File doesn't exist\n"); exit(1); } first_char = fgetc(fp); fgets(first_line, 80, fp); fclose(fp);. Second arg to fopen(): "r"/"rb" = read mode text/bin, "w"/"wb" = write mode, "a"/"ab" = append, "r+"/"r+b" = read/write.
notes_text: The C FILE* approach is the predecessor to C++ streams. While more verbose and error-prone (no RAII, manual NULL checks), it is still the standard for C programming and is used in many system-level APIs.

title: File Access (C Style)
summary: C file I/O functions include text access (fprintf, fscanf, fputc, fgetc, fputs, fgets) and binary access (fread, fwrite), with FILE* tracking position.
main_text: Many file I/O functions available in C. Text file access: fprintf(), fscanf(), fputc(), fgetc(), fputs(), fgets(). Binary file access: fread(), fwrite(). Your file pointer (FILE * var) implicitly keeps track of where you are in the file, just like the getp in C++ streams. EOF constant is returned when you hit the end of the file or you can use feof() which will return true or false. Example with file 'It was the best of...': fp starts at beginning, c = fgetc(fp) returns 'I' and advances fp. Successive reads advance through the file. At the end: while(!feof(fp)) // okay to access next byte of file { if((c = fgetc(fp)) != EOF) // process c }.
notes_text: The C-style file access functions mirror the C++ stream functions but use a procedural rather than object-oriented interface. fgetc is equivalent to get(), fprintf is equivalent to <<, and feof is equivalent to eof().

images.description: File content diagram showing 'It was the best of...' with fp positions. After fgetc(fp), fp advances one character. At end of file, fp points past last character and feof returns true.

title: Text File Input (C Style)
summary: C text input functions: fgetc() reads one character, fgets() reads a line up to \n, and fscanf() reads and converts ASCII to typed variables.
main_text: fgetc(): Get a single ASCII character from the file. fgets(): Get a line of text or a certain number of characters (up to and including \n). Stops at EOF. If EOF is first char read then the function returns NULL. Will append the NULL char at the end of the characters read. fscanf(): Read ASCII characters and convert to another variable type. Returns number of successful items read or 'EOF' if that is the first character read. These three functions provide increasing levels of abstraction: character-level (fgetc), line-level (fgets), and formatted (fscanf).
notes_text: fgets is safer than gets() (which was removed from the C standard due to buffer overflow vulnerabilities) because it takes a maximum character count. fscanf is the input counterpart to fprintf and works like scanf but reads from a file instead of stdin.

title: Text File Output (C Style)
summary: C text output functions: fputc() writes one character, fputs() writes a string, and fprintf() writes formatted text to a file.
main_text: fputc(): Write a single ASCII character to the file. fputs(): Write a text string to the file. fprintf(): Write the resulting text string to the file, with format specifiers for typed data (like printf but to a file). These three functions mirror the input functions: fputc is the output counterpart to fgetc, fputs to fgets, and fprintf to fscanf.
notes_text: fprintf is the most commonly used of these three functions because it handles formatted output with type conversion. It uses the same format specifiers as printf (%d, %f, %s, etc.) but writes to a FILE* instead of stdout.

title: Binary File I/O (C Style)
summary: C binary I/O uses fread() and fwrite() with pointers, element count, element size, and FILE pointer as arguments.
main_text: fread(): Pass a pointer to where you want the data read from the file to be placed in memory (e.g. &x if x is an int or data if data is an array). Pass the number of 'elements' to read then pass the size of each 'element'. Number of bytes read = number_of_elements * size_of_element. Pass the file pointer. fwrite(): Same argument scheme as fread(). Example: int main(int argc, char *argv[]) { int x; double data[10]; FILE *fp; fp = fopen("stuff.txt","r"); if(fp == NULL){ printf("File doesn't exist\n"); exit(1); } fread(&x, 1, sizeof(int), fp); fread(data, 10, sizeof(double), fp); fclose(fp); return 0; }.
notes_text: fread and fwrite are the C equivalents of istream::read and ostream::write. The argument order differs: C uses (ptr, count, size, file) while C++ uses (ptr, total_bytes). The C version separates element count and element size, which can be more intuitive.

title: Changing File Pointer Location (C Style)
summary: C uses fseek() with SEEK_SET/SEEK_CUR/SEEK_END to reposition the file pointer, and ftell() to get the current byte offset.
main_text: Rather than read/writing sequentially in a file we often need to jump around to particular byte locations. fseek(): Go to a particular byte location. Can be specified relative from current position or absolute byte from start or end of file. ftell(): Return the current location's byte-offset from the beginning of the file. Example: int main(int argc, char *argv[]) { int size; FILE *fp; fp = fopen("stuff.txt","r"); if(fp == NULL){ printf("File doesn't exist\n"); exit(1); } fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_END); size = ftell(fp); printf("File is %d bytes\n", size); fclose(fp); return 0; }. Third arg to fseek(): SEEK_SET = position from beginning of file, SEEK_CUR = position relative to current location, SEEK_END = position relative from end of file (i.e. negative number).
notes_text: fseek and ftell are the C equivalents of seekg and tellg. The constant names differ (SEEK_SET vs ios_base::beg, SEEK_CUR vs ios_base::cur, SEEK_END vs ios_base::end) but the semantics are identical.
